scoreNote: Strong (5): argues the policy's aim is just and economically wise, then weighs the cost and fairness consequences of the open-ended 'any', and shows careful design can preserve the promise while controlling cost; weighs the policy's effects.

sentences.text: A brilliant student wins a place at a great university, then turns it down because she cannot pay — a loss not only to her but to everyone.
To prevent such losses, the proposed policy would have governments offer a free university education to any student admitted to a university who cannot afford the tuition.

The policy is, in its aim, both just and wise, since talent wasted for lack of money is a loss to the whole society; but its sweeping form raises real questions of cost and fairness that a well-designed version must answer.

sections.role: Body — The case for the policy

sentences.text: The core of the policy is compelling.
When admission depends on ability but attendance depends on wealth, gifted students from poor families are shut out, and the nation loses the doctors, scientists, and thinkers they might have become.
Funding their education is not charity but investment, for an educated population repays the cost many times over in productivity, innovation, and taxes.
It also serves justice, ensuring that the doors of opportunity open by merit rather than by the accident of a family's bank balance.
On both grounds — fairness and the public good — the policy's aim is sound.

sections.role: Body — The cost and fairness concerns

sentences.text: However, the word any, and the open-ended cost it implies, demand careful thought.
A blanket promise to fund anyone admitted who cannot pay could become enormously expensive, straining public budgets and competing with other urgent needs like schools and hospitals.
It might also push universities to admit more students or to raise tuition, knowing the state will pay, inflating costs without improving education.
And cannot afford is slippery, since without careful definition subsidies could flow to families who could pay but prefer not to, wasting money meant for the truly needy.
The policy's generosity must be matched by discipline about cost and eligibility, or its strengths will be undone.

sections.role: Body — How to make it work

sentences.text: Moreover, these concerns argue for refining the policy, not abandoning it.
A sound version would means-test support carefully, perhaps cover tuition in return for later repayment once a graduate earns well, and tie funding to fields and institutions that serve the public.
Such measures keep the policy's central promise — that no admitted student is turned away for lack of money — while controlling its cost and protecting its fairness.
Many nations already fund higher education in roughly this way, proving that the goal is achievable without bankrupting the treasury.
The right response to the policy's risks is to design it well, not to deny able students the chance they have earned.
In conclusion, governments should help any admitted student who cannot afford university, for the policy's aim is both just and economically wise.

Wasting talent for lack of money harms everyone, so the policy is advantageous wherever it opens opportunity by merit; its dangers lie not in the goal but in an undisciplined design, which careful means-testing, repayment, and clear eligibility can readily address.
No student admitted on merit should be sent home for want of money — but the promise must be funded wisely, not blindly.
